messages.subject: Fitted values, marginals and inla.emarginal
parts:
Hi,

I have a spatio-temporal model mod1 (see the call at the end). If I multiply the exponentiated mean fixed marginal and all the exponentiated mean random marginals, the result is similar although not equal to the mean fitted values:

> summary(mod1$summary.fitted.values$mean)
    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
 0.01288  0.19806  0.59215  1.55649  1.21165 65.16249 
> summary(exp(mod1$summary.fixed[1, 1]) *
+               exp(rep(mod1$summary.random$id_state$mean, e = 17)) *
+               exp(rep(mod1$summary.random$id_state2$mean, e = 17)) *
+               exp(rep(mod1$summary.random$id_year$mean, 27)) *
+               exp(rep(mod1$summary.random$id_year2$mean, 27)) *
+               exp(mod1$summary.random$id_state_year$mean))
    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
 0.01058  0.18136  0.57124  1.54370  1.19794 65.13050

If I exponentiate with inla.emarginal, the result is very different to the mean fitted values:

> fie <- function(x) inla.emarginal(exp, x)
> summary(sapply(mod1$marginals.fixed, fie) *
+           rep(sapply(mod1$marginals.random$id_state, fie), e = 17) *
+           rep(sapply(mod1$marginals.random$id_state2, fie), e = 17) *
+           rep(sapply(mod1$marginals.random$id_year, fie), 27) *
+           rep(sapply(mod1$marginals.random$id_year2, fie), 27) *
+           sapply(mod1$marginals.random$id_state_year, fie))
     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
  0.02498   0.27218   0.83381   2.61385   1.86217 118.46717

Should not be this last multiplication equal to the mean fitted values?

> mod1

Call:
c("inla(formula = cases ~ 1 + f(id_state, model = \"besag\", hyper = prec, ",  "    graph = br_adj, constr = TRUE, scale.model = TRUE) + f(id_state2, ",  "    model = \"iid\", hyper = prec, constr = TRUE) + f(id_year, ",  "    model = \"rw1\", hyper = prec, constr = TRUE) + f(id_year2, ",  "    model = \"iid\", hyper = prec, constr = TRUE) + f(id_state_year, ",  "    model = \"iid\", hyper = prec, constr = TRUE), family = \"poisson\", ",  "    data = lepto, E = expected_cases, lincomb = lcs, control.compute = list(dic = TRUE), ",  "    control.predictor = list(link = 1, compute = TRUE))")

Time used:
 Pre-processing    Running inla Post-processing           Total 
      0.3354988       4.0455093       0.1156979       4.4967060 

Integration Strategy: Model contains 5 hyperparameters
The model contains 1 fixed effect (including a possible intercept)

Likelihood model: poisson

The model has 5 random effects:
1.'id_state' is a Besags ICAR model

2.'id_state2' is a IID model

3.'id_year' is a RW1 model

4.'id_year2' is a IID model

5.'id_state_year' is a IID model

Best regards,
Oswaldo

On 4 Nov 2017, at 13:06, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

No, E(f(x))  (your second calculation) is not the same thing as f(E(x)) (your first calculation) for nonlinear f().

...and your second calculation isn’t quite doing E(f(x)) either, since you’re taking the product of expectations and not the expectation of the product.

Finn

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Fitted values, marginals and inla.emarginal
parts:
On Sat, 2017-11-04 at 05:59 -0700, Oswaldo Santos Baquero wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I have a spatio-temporal model mod1 (see the call at the end). If I
> multiply the exponentiated mean fixed marginal and all the
> exponentiated mean random marginals, the result is similar although
> not equal to the mean fitted values:

Thanks for your email.

Let x1 and x2 to be random variables, then

E(x1 + x2) = E(x1) + E(x2)

is valid always (as long as its exists), but

E(exp(x1+x2)) \not= E(exp(x1)) E(exp(x2))

in general, and equal only if independent.

your last part with inla.emarginal, I do not understand....

H



--
Håvard Rue

parts:
Thanks for your quick reply.
I though that inla.emarginal(exp, x) and exp were somehow alternative ways to exponentiate the marginals, but the first was recommended just to avoid biases with distributions that are note invariant to transformations. Therefore, in the previous example I used inla.emargian just as an alternative to exp. Now, I realized that I was doing different calculations, not simply exponentiating with different functions.
